title: Mourning girlfriend questions SIU account of killing
subtitle: After watchdog clears police in Port Perry slaying, a Durham woman wants answers.
article: In the days after she witnessed her boyfriend Gerald Rattu being shot and killed by police, Laurie Bailey said, she would see and hear the scene every time she closed her eyes.
"I'll never get it out of my mind: 'Drop it now! Drop it now! Pop. Pop,' " she told the Star last week, referring to the gunshots she heard as Rattu, 59, walked down the driveway with a knife.

What Bailey remembers differs significantly with the version of events published late last month by Ontario's police watchdog, the Special Investigations Unit, which declined to lay charges against the unnamed Durham Regional Police officer who shot Rattu.
The Bowmanville resident is now determined to make public what she says is the truth of what really happened on the evening of Jan. 16.
She was in Port Perry house-sitting for her sister. Rattu, who she had been seeing for about three years, was staying with her.
Rattu would never have harmed anyone, she said. Although they didn't live together, Bailey recalls Rattu would do things like cut her lawn and do the dishes while she was at work.
"I didn't like it when he did the laundry, but he did that too," she said with a laugh.
While at work that afternoon in January, she started getting what she described as "weird" text messages from Rattu, and noticed he was also posting strange statements on Facebook.
"I knew he had been drinking," she said.
When Bailey got home that evening, she prepared something for him to eat and told him she wanted to take a break.
"I said I just wanted some time to myself," she said. "We were arguing about it. I just wanted a little break, a little space. And it just escalated. Then he got a hold of the knife."
She said Rattu first grabbed a butcher knife.

"He didn't wave it at me or anything," Bailey said. "I managed to get it away from him. I cut my hand doing it, but I kicked it under the couch so he couldn't get at it. I'm trying to block him from getting back into the kitchen to get another one."

But she said Rattu managed to push past her and did indeed get another knife. At one point Bailey's niece called 911 and she and her boyfriend came up from the basement and fled, telling Bailey to get out.
Bailey then called 911 herself, saying that she specifically told the operator that Rattu was intoxicated and was going to harm himself.
"I stayed on the porch until police arrived," she said. "The police car comes, parks on the street, and the cop was standing behind the car."
She said Rattu "calmly" walked past her while she was standing on the porch, and that he began walking down the driveway with the knife in his right hand, pointed toward himself.
Sitting in her living room last week, Bailey dissected the information published by the SIU in its news release last month about what happened next.

According to SIU director Tony Loparco, the officer was unable to stall Rattu until another officer arrived with a Taser. The director said the officer considered use-of-force alternatives such as his baton or pepper spray, but realized neither would have worked in that situation.
Loparco noted that aside from holding a knife, Rattu was "physically imposing," and displaying hostility and combativeness.
"The officer was faced with a dangerous and dynamic situation that unfolded quickly over a mere 52 seconds," Loparco wrote.

"His fear for his own safety was both subjectively and objectively reasonable and his actions were directed towards self-preservation. His decision to fire his gun was reasonable in the circumstances, and he only did so when he had no other options."
First of all, Bailey disputes that the officer ever walked up the driveway before shooting Rattu.
"He was at the cruiser, behind the trunk, the whole time," she said.
She also disputes hearing Rattu say to the officer words to the effect of "shoot me" and "kill me."
"He didn't say a word," she said.
According to the SIU, the officer, upon arriving at the scene, yelled "Police - don't move, drop the knife," and that he continued to issue the police challenge.
But Bailey is adamant that all she heard from the porch is "Drop it now, drop it now" and then two gunshots.

She also wants to know the identities of the nine civilian witnesses interviewed as part of the SIU investigation. She said it's possible neighbours looked through their window after the shooting, but says she saw no one else outside when the shooting actually happened.

The witnesses' statements would be included in the full SIU director's report, which is only given to the Attorney General and never released to the public. (An independent review of police oversight bodies in Ontario is currently looking at whether these reports should be made public.)
The report would also indicate all the evidence gathered by the SIU as part of its investigation, and potentially include how the director weighed the statements of some witnesses versus others.
SIU spokeswoman Monica Hudon declined to comment on Bailey's claims because a coroner's inquest could potentially be called in the case.

She said Loparco's decision not to lay charges "was premised on the full body of evidence collected. This included interviews of nine separate civilian witnesses, as well as five witness officers and the subject officer. The SIU also reviewed the police communication recordings, the post-mortem results and physical evidence collected at the scene."
A spokesman for Durham police said the force does not comment on SIU investigations.
"This incident was thoroughly investigated by an independent body and no fault was found," said Dave Selby.
Bailey also took issue with the fact that she was never notified about Loparco's decision - she learned about it after her daughter saw it in the news.

"I was at their beck and call whenever they needed to ask questions, but they didn't have the courtesy to tell me," she said. "I guess they must have told the family, but hey, I was the one there who witnessed it. They could have called me to let me know that this was going to be printed."
She said she was angry when she saw the SIU's findings. "It just reopened everything in my mind," she said.

Hudon at the SIU said the agency's policy in death cases is to notify the next of kin, and that in this case, Rattu's father, three siblings and one sibling-in-law were notified in person a week before the news release was issued.
Bailey has gone through counselling since the shooting, and has had to take medication for anxiety.
"I was hysterical," after the shooting, she said. "I couldn't breathe."
She said she knew Rattu was dead after the shooting. She tried to see his body at the hospital, but never did get to see him again.
"The last memory is of him lying on the ground."
